---
title: "2. Normalization and highly variable genes"
---

## The problem normalization solves

Two otherwise similar cells can have different total UMI counts simply because one cell was captured/sequenced more deeply.

Suppose:

- Cell A: 5,000 total UMIs; CD3D = 50
- Cell B: 10,000 total UMIs; CD3D = 100

The raw CD3D counts differ twofold, but CD3D occupies the same fraction of each library. Standard log normalization therefore performs a cell-level library-size correction followed by a log transform.

For Seurat's default `LogNormalize`, conceptually:

$$
\operatorname{normalized}_{g,c}
= \log\left(1 + \frac{x_{g,c}}{\sum_{g'} x_{g',c}} \times 10{,}000\right)
$$

```r
obj <- NormalizeData(obj, normalization.method = "LogNormalize", scale.factor = 10000)
```

### What normalization does *not* do

It does not remove batch effects, make donors biological replicates, eliminate dropout, or make genes comparable for PCA. Those are separate issues.

## Highly variable genes (HVGs)

PCA usually should not be driven by thousands of genes that barely change across cells. `FindVariableFeatures()` identifies genes with more variability than expected for their average expression.

```r
obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000)
VariableFeaturePlot(obj)
```

The key idea is the **mean–variance relationship**: highly expressed genes tend to have greater raw variance even when nothing interesting is happening. HVG methods model that relationship and prioritize features that vary unusually strongly.

### HVG does not mean "important gene"

A gene can be biologically essential but nearly constant across all cells. It would be poor for distinguishing cells and therefore may not be selected as an HVG. Conversely, a highly variable gene can reflect technical or stress-associated variation.

## Example

If ACTB is high in nearly every immune cell, it contributes little to distinguishing T cells from B cells. If CD3D, MS4A1, and LST1 differ strongly among populations, they are far more informative for cell-state representation.

## SCTransform

SCTransform is an alternative normalization/variance-stabilization strategy that models UMI counts with a regularized negative-binomial framework. It can replace the classic `NormalizeData()` → `FindVariableFeatures()` → `ScaleData()` preprocessing sequence in many workflows. The workshop starts with the classic workflow because its individual transformations are easier to learn explicitly.

::: {.callout-note}
Do not mix conceptual questions. "Which cells have different library depths?" is normalization. "Which genes vary unusually across cells?" is feature selection.
:::
